asl: PISA 2012 Released Items, Mathematics: DRIP RATE (PM903Q01, PM903Q03)
stimul:
Botir, a farmer in the Fergana Valley, waters his orchard by drip irrigation. A dripper under each tree releases water drop by drop. Agronomists calculate the drip rate of a dripper with the following formula:

$D = \dfrac{k \cdot V}{60 \cdot t}$

where D is the number of drops per minute, k is the number of drops in 1 liter of water, V is the volume of water given to one tree (liters), and t is the watering time (hours).

Model: SH-90
Tower height: 120 meters
Number of blades: 3
Length of one blade: 45 meters
Maximum rotation speed: 15 revolutions per minute
Construction cost: 36 billion soums
Income: 450 soums for every 1 kWh produced
Maintenance cost: 27 soums for every 1 kWh produced
Efficiency: operates 95% of the time in a year

Note: a kilowatt-hour (kWh) is a unit of electrical energy.

asl: PISA 2015 Science (P15S): Bird Migration (S656), 3 savol
stimul:
Crane Migration

Every year many birds fly from the places where they nest to the places where they spend the winter, and back again — this is called migration. Every spring and autumn thousands of birds, including cranes, pass over Uzbekistan. Each year volunteer observers count the passing birds at set locations, for example around the Aydar-Arnasay lakes. Scientists also catch some of the birds, put a numbered ring on their leg, and release them. Together, the places where ringed birds are seen and the volunteers' counts help to work out the birds' migration routes.

Most small songbirds fly at night, not during the day, when they migrate. During the day they rest and feed.

The two schematic maps in the picture show the routes of one species of crane, drawn from more than ten years of observations: Map 1 — autumn routes flying south, Map 2 — spring routes returning north. The thicker the arrow, the larger the flock that flies along that route.

asl: PISA 2015 Science (P15S): Meteoroids and Craters (S641), 4 savol
stimul:
Meteoroids and Craters

Pieces of rock and iron moving through space are called meteoroids. When a meteoroid comes close to a planet or a moon, it is pulled toward it. If the planet has an atmosphere, the meteoroid heats up from friction with the air, burns, and leaves a bright trail in the sky — we call it a “shooting star”. Many meteoroids burn up completely in the atmosphere. Those that do not burn up in time hit the surface and make a hollow — a crater.

At the Maidanak Observatory in the Samarkand region, astronomers observe craters on the Moon's surface. The Moon has almost no atmosphere, so its surface is full of craters. Venus's atmosphere, on the other hand, is about 90 times denser than Earth's.

The picture shows three craters on the Moon's surface — K, L, and M — seen from above.

stimul:
A Study of Mountain Slopes

In a ravine in the Zomin mountains, students noticed an interesting difference: the north-facing slope of the ravine was densely covered with juniper trees and shrubs, while plants on the south-facing slope were sparse.

The students decided to investigate the reason for this difference. For one month they measured three factors on each slope:
• Solar radiation — how much solar energy reaches the place;
• Soil moisture — the proportion of water in the soil;
• Precipitation — how much rain falls on the place.

On each slope, two identical measuring instruments for each factor were set up in different places.

The students calculated the mean of the instrument readings and recorded the measurement uncertainty using the “±” sign:

Slope | Solar radiation | Soil moisture | Precipitation
North | 4100 ± 350 MJ/m² | 31 ± 3 % | 520 ± 45 mm
South | 7600 ± 450 MJ/m² | 17 ± 2 % | 545 ± 50 mm

nom: A Fish Farm on the Syr Darya
asl: PISA 2015 Science (P15S): Sustainable Fish Farming (S601), 3 savol
stimul:
A Sustainable Fish Farm

People's demand for fish keeps growing, and this puts heavy pressure on wild fish in rivers and lakes. That is why an experimental farm on the Syr Darya is testing a sustainable way of raising common carp.

A sustainable farm must solve two problems: (1) growing food for the fish on the farm itself and (2) keeping the water clean. Fish waste builds up in the water and harms the fish themselves. River water flows through the farm all the time; before the water goes back to the river, the waste and excess nutrients in it (substances that algae and plants need to grow) must be removed.

The farm has three ponds (see the diagram). Water flows from Pond 1 to Pond 2, then to Pond 3, and returns to the river.

The farm uses the following organisms:
• Carp — the fish being raised; its favorite food is daphnia.
• Microalgae — microscopic algae that grow with only light and nutrients (they are already in Pond 1).
• Daphnia (water fleas) — tiny crustaceans that feed on microalgae and reproduce very quickly.
• Mussels — shelled animals that pass water through their bodies and feed on the microalgae and tiny particles in it.
• Reeds — plants that absorb nutrients and waste from the water.

nom: The Ladybug — Protector of Cotton Fields
asl: PISA 2025 Science (P25S): Black Soldier Fly, 3 savol
stimul:
The Ladybug — Protector of Cotton Fields

The ladybug is a small beetle with black spots on its red or yellow wing cases. It is common in the orchards and fields of Uzbekistan.

Ladybugs and their larvae feed on aphids (tiny sap-sucking insects). Aphids suck the sap of cotton plants, vegetables, and fruit trees, causing great damage to crops. A single ladybug larva eats several hundred aphids during its development.

At biofactories (biolaboratories), ladybugs are bred and their larvae are released into the fields. This is a way of fighting pests without poisonous chemicals.

One female ladybug lays several hundred eggs during her life. The body of a ladybug larva is covered by a hard outer covering (exoskeleton), and the larva molts several times as it grows. The picture shows the life cycle of the ladybug.

asl: PISA 2025 Science (P25S): Fast Fashion, 3 savol
stimul:
Cotton and “Fast Fashion”

Many people are worried about the effect on the environment of producing clothes and throwing away old ones. The habit of buying cheap clothes often and throwing them away quickly is called “fast fashion.”

Cotton fiber comes from the surface of the seeds inside the cotton boll. Compared with synthetic fibers, cotton fiber needs less processing and breaks down more quickly in nature.

However, growing cotton requires a lot of water, fertilizer, pesticides, and other chemicals. In Uzbekistan, taking large amounts of water from the Amu Darya and Syr Darya to irrigate cotton fields has been one of the main causes of the drying of the Aral Sea. To reduce these problems, sustainable methods of growing cotton are being developed.

For a crop to be recognized as “organic,” it must be grown without synthetic fertilizers and pesticides; genetically modified varieties are not considered organic either.

nom: A Wind Farm in the Desert
asl: PISA 2025 Science (P25S): Offshore Wind Turbine Farm, 3 savol
stimul:
A Wind Farm in the Desert

A district administration is considering building a wind farm in a desert area. The wind turns the turbine blades, the turbine generates electricity, and the electricity is sent through a cable to the main power grid. At present the district gets its electricity mainly from thermal power stations that burn coal and gas.

Some of the district's residents support the project, while others are worried that it will harm the local natural environment.

The wind farm will be built in one of the four zones in the picture. The farther a zone is from the power grid, the more expensive it is to lay the cable and build roads.
• Zone A — every spring and autumn, very large flocks of birds fly low over this area.
• Zone B — home to rare (endemic) plants that grow only in this area.
• Zones C and D — common animals such as gerbils and lizards live here; they can easily move to neighboring areas.

nom: Why did the Aral Sea dry up?
asl: PISA 2018 Reading, Unit CR551: Rapa Nui (blog + kitob taqrizi + ilmiy jurnal maqolasi)
stimul:
Scenario. Geographer Dilnoza Rahimova is coming to your school to give a talk about her field research on the shores of the Aral Sea. To prepare for the talk, you are reading three sources.

SOURCE 1. A professor's blog — “A Geographer's Diary” (geographersdiary.uz/field/moynaq)

May 23, 11:22
This morning I looked out of the window of the house I am renting in Moynaq. In the distance, a salt flat lies white, saxaul and camelthorn bushes sway in the wind, the sky is clear, and on the horizon you can see the steep cliffs of the Ustyurt Plateau.

I feel a little sad, knowing this is my last week here. I have finished my fieldwork and will soon return to Tashkent. Later today I will go to the ship graveyard on the edge of town to say goodbye to the rusting ships I have studied for the past nine months.

If you have been following my blog, you know that Moynaq was once a busy port. In the 1960s, a fish cannery operated here, and boats went out to sea every day. Today the water is more than 100 kilometers from the town.

For many years, tourists who came to Moynaq wondered how the ships ended up sitting on the sand. Some thought a powerful storm had thrown them onto land. In the 1990s, a group of geographers, together with local fishermen, compared old maps and satellite images and showed that the ships had not moved at all; instead, the water had retreated away from them. That is how the mystery of the ships was solved.

However, another mystery still remains. Why did the sea dry up almost completely in such a short time — in only half a century? When I look out of my window, where waves once broke I see only sand and salt. We will explore this puzzle in my next posts and talks. For now, I suggest you start with Akmal Nurmatov's book “The Dried-Up Sea.” This review of the book is a good place to begin.

Comments:
Traveler_14 (May 24, 16:31): Hello, professor! I read your posts about the Aral with great interest. I can't wait to read “The Dried-Up Sea”!
AralFan_KB (May 25, 09:07): I really like your observations about the Aral. But I think another theory should also be considered. Try reading this article: sciencenow.uz/aral-climate

SOURCE 2. Book review — “The Dried-Up Sea” (bookreviews.uz)

Akmal Nurmatov's new book, “The Dried-Up Sea,” is a serious warning about what happens when people treat nature carelessly. The book describes several lakes and rivers that have changed dramatically because of human activity. One of the most tragic examples in the book is the Aral Sea.

The author writes that in 1960 the Aral was the fourth-largest lake in the world, with an area of almost 68 thousand square kilometers. The sea fed thousands of fishermen, and port towns such as Moynaq and Aralsk flourished. Starting in the 1960s, a large part of the water of the Amu Darya and Syr Darya rivers was diverted through canals to irrigate cotton and rice fields. By the 2000s, the sea level had dropped by more than 20 meters, the water had become very salty, and the fish had almost disappeared. In Nurmatov's opinion, the wasteful use of water on the fields led to the destruction of the sea.

The lesson of this remarkable but terrifying book is that it is people themselves who decide to change nature, and people who are able to save it. With hope, the author also tells the story of the Kokaral Dam, built in 2005 to save the Small Aral. The book is skillfully written, and everyone who loves nature should read it.

SOURCE 3. Popular science magazine article — “Was cotton alone to blame for drying up the Aral?” (sciencenow.uz/aral-climate)
Author: Botir Qodirov, science writer

In 2009, geographer Akmal Nurmatov published the book “The Dried-Up Sea.” In it, he also told the history of the fishing towns on the Aral coast, Moynaq and Aralsk.

After the book came out, a heated debate began. Some scientists questioned Nurmatov's theory about what happened to the Aral. They agree that the amount of river water reaching the Aral fell sharply after the 1960s, that is, after the period when the Moynaq cannery was at its peak. However, they disagree with Nurmatov about the cause of the decrease in water.

Recently, two scientists — hydrologist Laylo Karimova and climatologist Sardor Yoldoshev — announced a new theory. In their view, the main cause is the climate becoming drier: there has been less snow and rain in the mountains where the rivers begin, and in hot years more water has evaporated from rivers and fields. As a result, the rivers have carried much less water to the sea than before. The scientists believe that the Aral also became shallower naturally several times in the past.

In summer, the air temperature on the Aral coast rises above 40 °C, and in such heat a great deal of water evaporates from an open water surface. To support their theory, Karimova and Yoldoshev point to the remains of the 14th-century Kerderi Mausoleum, found in 2001 on the dried-up seabed: this means that in the Middle Ages the sea level was much lower than in 1960. Of course, they admit that irrigation also played a role in the drying of the Aral. But they consider the climate to be even more to blame.

Note: the blog, book, review, article and the people in them were invented for learning purposes. The information about the port of Moynaq and its ship graveyard, the area of the Aral in 1960, the Kokaral Dam and the Kerderi Mausoleum is real.

Hello! Yesterday three of my six 3-week-old chicks started sneezing, their eyes are watery, and one of them did not eat any grain at all today. I have an antibiotic at home that I take myself. Can I crush it and add it to the chicks' water? The district veterinary clinic is closed until Monday, and the emergency number is not answering. I'm afraid the other chicks will catch it too, and I need to do something for them before Monday. Thanks in advance!

I think you shouldn't rush. Last year my neighbor gave her ducks her own medicine, and the ducks got even worse. Since then, I give my birds any medicine only after a vet tells me to.

Last spring my chicks were sneezing in exactly the same way. I crushed a little of the antibiotic I had at home and added it to their water, and they got better in two days! Just don't give them too much — an overdose can be harmful. I hope your chicks get well soon!

Poultry_Bazaar — November 14, 20:02
Hi! Don't miss our big discounts on feed, vitamins and equipment for poultry! This week, all products are 30 percent off!

Bobur_T — November 14, 20:15
My hens have stopped laying eggs as winter approaches. Does anyone have any advice?

Hello, Dilfuza! I am a veterinarian specializing in poultry diseases. Do not give your chicks medicine made for people on your own: its ingredients and dose are not designed for birds. Veterinary pharmacies sell special medicines for chicks. According to the handbook “Poultry Diseases,” such a medicine is added to the drinking water, and the amount is calculated from the chicks' live weight: it states exactly how many milligrams to give per kilogram of body weight. For now, separate the sick chicks from the healthy ones and keep them in a warm, dry place. On Monday, be sure to show them to your vet. I hope they recover!

“Oqsoy” products help you lose weight and maintain a healthy weight. They strengthen bones and teeth and improve heart health. A glass of “Oqsoy” milk is a treasure of vitamins, minerals and health!

According to pediatrician Rano Aliyeva, PhD in medicine, milk brings together many substances the body needs. The Association of Dairy Producers also supports this view and stresses that many health experts agree:

“Milk is a complete package of important nutrients for the body. It is an excellent source of calcium, protein and potassium, and it contains B vitamins. Doctors recommend dairy products. The role of dairy products in a healthy diet is recognized by many nutrition experts and medical organizations.”
— Association of Dairy Producers, 2019

SOURCE 2. Article on the “Healthy Life” health portal — “Is it time to say ‘no’ to milk?”
Author: health writer and doctor N. Ganiyeva

In Uzbekistan, milk and dairy products are an essential part of every meal: tea with milk in the morning, yogurt at lunch, ayran in the evening. We have grown up hearing, “If you drink milk, your bones will be strong.” However, in recent years, more and more researchers have begun to question this belief.

For many years, milk producers have promoted drinking several glasses of milk a day. But a number of studies in the past decade have cast doubt on milk's ability to strengthen bones and on other claims. The results may surprise you.

One such study was published in 2014 in the respected “British Medical Journal.” More than 100 thousand people in Sweden were followed for 11–20 years. In women who drank a lot of milk, bone fractures did not decrease — on the contrary, they were slightly more common. In addition, among men and women who drank a lot of milk, the proportion who died during the study period was also higher.

According to scientists' estimates, in about two-thirds of the world's adults, the ability to digest lactose — milk sugar — decreases with age. In such people, drinking milk can cause bloating and stomach pain.

Of course, these are serious claims, and many more studies are needed to confirm them. The authors of the study themselves stressed that the results of an observational study do not prove cause and effect. However, there is growing evidence that milk is not as healthy as we thought. If these claims become undeniable facts, it may be time to say “no” to cow's milk.

Note: the “Oqsoy” farm, the association, the doctors and the “Healthy Life” portal are invented. The information about the 2014 Swedish study and about lactose is real.

asl: Take the Test, Mathematics unit 15: Science Tests
stimul: At Sardor's school, the physics teacher grades tests on a 100-point scale. Sardor scored an average of 72 points on the first five tests. On the sixth test he got 90 points.

asl: Take the Test, Mathematics unit 16: Bookshelves
stimul:
In a furniture workshop, making one chair requires:

4 legs,
1 seat,
1 backrest,
12 screws,
4 metal brackets.

The storeroom has 58 legs, 16 seats, 15 backrests, 160 screws and 60 metal brackets.

asl: Take the Test, Mathematics unit 17: Litter
stimul:
For a biology project, students collected information about the approximate life spans of some animals:

Animal | Approximate life span
Silk moth | 1–2 weeks
House mouse | 1–2 years
Sheep | 10–12 years
Horse | 25–30 years
Asian elephant | 60–70 years
Giant tortoise | more than 100 years

A student wants to show this information in a bar chart.

asl: Take the Test, Mathematics unit 18: Earthquake
stimul:
A science program on television discussed whether earthquakes can be predicted. A seismologist on the program gave the following hypothetical example:

“The probability that a strong earthquake will occur in the city of Yangiobod in the next thirty years is two out of three.”

(Yangiobod is a made-up city name.)

asl: Take the Test, Mathematics unit 19: Choices
stimul: A small café in Samarkand sells plain vanilla ice cream. If customers wish, they can choose toppings to sprinkle on it. The café has four kinds of toppings: chopped nuts, chocolate chips, raisins and strawberry jam.

asl: Take the Test, Mathematics unit 20: Test Scores
stimul:
A school held a qualifying test for the mathematics olympiad. The test is out of 100 points, and a student who scores 50 points or more qualifies. The chart shows the results of classes 9A and 9B (12 students from each class).

The average score of class 9A is 61.5, and that of class 9B is 64.0.

Looking at the chart, the teacher said: “Class 9B did better than class 9A on this test.” The students of 9A disagreed and want to show that 9B did not necessarily do better.

asl: Take the Test, Mathematics unit 21: Skateboard
stimul:
Javohir is a cycling fan. He looked at the prices at the “Velomarkaz” shop in Tashkent. At the shop you can buy a ready-made bike, or buy four parts separately and assemble the bike yourself: a frame, a wheel set, a chain and gear set, and a brake and handlebar set.

Item — Price (soums)
Ready-made bike — 2 150 000 or 2 400 000
Frame — 900 000, 1 200 000 or 1 350 000
Wheel set (2 wheels) — 380 000 or 720 000
Chain and gear set — 450 000
Brake and handlebar set (brakes, handlebar, cables) — 210 000 or 400 000

(The shop name and prices are hypothetical.)

asl: Take the Test, Mathematics unit 22: Staircase
stimul: A staircase going down underground was built at a new metro station in Tashkent. The staircase has 24 identical steps; its total height is 3.84 m and its total length (horizontally) is 7.20 m (see the picture).

asl: Take the Test, Mathematics unit 23: Number Cubes
stimul:
A die used in backgammon (narda) is a cube with 1 to 6 dots on its faces. There is a rule for dice:

The total number of dots on two opposite faces is always 7.

Nodir wants to make a die out of cardboard. He cuts, folds and glues the cardboard. The picture shows four nets (I, II, III, IV) that fold into a cube, with dots drawn on their squares.

nom: Polls on the New Park Project
asl: Take the Test, Mathematics unit 24: Support for the President
stimul:
On March 22, the residents of a city will vote on a project to build a new central park. To find out what percentage of residents support the project, four news outlets each carried out a poll (the outlets are hypothetical):

Outlet 1: 52.5% — poll on March 2, among 500 randomly selected residents who are eligible to vote.
Outlet 2: 57.0% — poll on March 18, among 500 randomly selected residents who are eligible to vote.
Outlet 3: 55.0% — poll on March 18, among 1000 randomly selected residents who are eligible to vote.
Outlet 4: 63.5% — poll on March 18, among 1500 subscribers of a Telegram channel who chose to vote.

nom: The Best Smartphone of the Year
asl: Take the Test, Mathematics unit 25: The Best Car
stimul:
A technology magazine rates new smartphones and gives the title “Smartphone of the Year” to the one with the highest total score. Six smartphones were rated (the names are hypothetical). The ratings:

Smartphone — Camera (K) — Battery (B) — Screen (E) — Value for money (N)
Alfa — 3 — 3 — 1 — 1
Beta — 2 — 2 — 2 — 2
Gamma — 3 — 2 — 3 — 2
Delta — 1 — 3 — 3 — 3
Omega — 2 — 1 — 3 — 3
Ramz — 2 — 3 — 2 — 3

Meaning of the ratings: 3 points — excellent, 2 points — good, 1 point — satisfactory.

asl: Take the Test, Mathematics unit 26: Step Pattern
stimul: A seller at Chorsu Bazaar stacks pomegranates on the counter in layers. The picture shows the first three stages: stage 1 has 1 pomegranate, stage 2 has 3, and stage 3 has 6. At each stage, the bottom row has one more pomegranate.

asl: Take the Test, Mathematics unit 27: Lichen
stimul:
As the Aral Sea dried up, a new desert, the Aralkum, appeared on its former seabed. Scientists have observed that salt-tolerant shrubs begin to grow about 5 years after the water retreats from a place. Seen from above, each shrub is roughly circular.

Suppose that the relationship between the diameter of a shrub and the time since the water retreated is given by the following approximate formula:

$d = 12\sqrt{t-5}$, $t \ge 5$,

where $d$ is the diameter of the shrub (in centimeters) and $t$ is the number of years since the water retreated. (The formula has been simplified for teaching purposes.)

asl: Take the Test, Mathematics unit 28: Coins
Take the Test, Mathematics unit 29: Pizzas
stimul: A pastry shop sells two kinds of round cake of the same height, made from the same recipe. The small cake has a diameter of 20 cm and costs 120 000 soums. The large cake has a diameter of 30 cm and costs 180 000 soums.

nom: Three Flower Beds in a Park
asl: Take the Test, Mathematics unit 30: Shapes
stimul: A landscape designer drew plans for three flower beds (A, B and C) for a new park. All three drawings are at the same scale. Flower bed B is a circle; the borders of flower beds A and C are wavy and irregular.

asl: Take the Test, Mathematics unit 31: Braking
stimul:
The stopping distance of a moving car consists of two parts:
• reaction distance — the distance the car travels from the moment the driver sees a hazard until the brake is pressed;
• braking distance — the distance traveled from the moment the brake is pressed until the car comes to a complete stop.

A table in a driving school manual gives approximate values calculated for good conditions (an alert driver, working brakes and tires, dry asphalt).

Speed — Reaction distance — Total stopping distance — Stopping time
50 km/h — 13.9 m — 27.7 m — 2.98 s
60 km/h — 16.7 m — 36.5 m — 3.38 s
70 km/h — 19.4 m — 46.5 m — 3.78 s
80 km/h — 22.2 m — 57.5 m — 4.17 s
90 km/h — 25 m — 69.6 m — 4.57 s
100 km/h — 27.8 m — 82.9 m — 4.97 s
110 km/h — 30.6 m — 97.2 m — 5.37 s
120 km/h — 33.3 m — 112.7 m — 5.76 s
130 km/h — 36.1 m — 129.3 m — 6.16 s

asl: Take the Test, Mathematics unit 32: Patio
stimul: Akmal wants to lay tiles on the rectangular porch of his new house. The porch is 4.75 m long and 3.20 m wide. Each square meter needs 64 tiles.

nom: The Amount of Medicine in the Blood
asl: Take the Test, Mathematics unit 33: Drug Concentrations
stimul:
At a hospital, a patient was given an injection of an antibiotic. The body gradually breaks down the medicine: one hour after the injection, only 75% of the medicine remains active. This process continues: at the end of each hour, 75% of the active medicine present at the end of the previous hour remains.

Second situation: Bahodir aka takes 150 mg of medicine to control his blood pressure. The graph shows the initial amount of the medicine and the active amount left in his blood after one, two, three and four days (see the graph).

nom: How the Aral Sea Is Shrinking
asl: Take the Test, Reading unit 1: Lake Chad
stimul:
Figure 1 shows how the surface area of the Aral Sea has changed over the years. Until the 1960s, the Aral was one of the largest lakes in the world, and for many years its area stayed almost the same, at about 68 thousand km². From that time on, a large share of the water of the Amu Darya and Syr Darya was diverted to irrigate cotton and rice fields, and the amount of water reaching the sea dropped sharply. In 1989, the sea split into two parts: the Small Aral in the north and the Large Aral in the south.

Figure 2 shows which fish species were recorded in which years in the reports of fishing enterprises in the southern part of the Aral. As the sea shrank, its water became saltier, and fish adapted to fresh water could not survive in it. In the 1980s, flounder, a fish that tolerates salt water, was brought to the sea.

The data in the figures have been rounded and simplified.

nom: Flu Vaccination at School: A Notice
asl: Take the Test, Reading unit 2: Flu
stimul:
(The following notice is fictional. It was posted on the board in the staff room by Dilnoza Karimova, a human resources officer at a school in Tashkent.)

[At the top of the notice there is a drawing of a smiling Grandfather Frost wearing a scarf. The text is divided into sections with large colorful headings, and in the bottom corner there is the line “Stay healthy!” and a little heart.]

READY FOR WINTER? LET’S STAY HEALTHY TOGETHER!

Dear colleagues! Every winter, the flu “pays a visit” to our school: several teachers fall ill on the same day, lessons get rescheduled, and we ourselves spend a week or two in bed.

What can we do?
The most reliable defense against the flu is a strong body. Walking in fresh air, getting enough sleep, and eating more fruit and vegetables help our bodies fight the virus. This year, the school administration is offering an extra option: a free flu vaccination.

When and where?
A nurse from the district family clinic will carry out vaccinations in the school medical room on one day during the week of November 14–18. The vaccination will take place during school hours, so you do not need to stay after classes. Participation is voluntary. Those being vaccinated will fill in a consent form confirming that they have no allergies and understand that mild side effects are possible.

Is it dangerous?
Doctors explain that you cannot catch the flu from the vaccine. Sometimes there may be a day or two of weakness, a slight rise in temperature, or soreness where the injection was given.

Who can be vaccinated?
Anyone who wants to be protected from the flu.
It is especially recommended for people over 60 and, regardless of age, for anyone with heart or lung disease or diabetes. All of us who work with hundreds of children every day are at risk of catching an illness.

Who should not be vaccinated?
People allergic to eggs, people who currently have a fever, and pregnant women. If you take medication regularly or have had a bad reaction to a vaccination before, consult your doctor first.

How can I sign up?
Tell Dilnoza Karimova by Friday, November 7. The exact day will be set according to the nurse’s schedule and the number of participants. If you want to be vaccinated this winter but cannot come that week, let Dilnoza know anyway: if enough people sign up, we will arrange another day.

Questions? Contact Dilnoza Karimova, extension 214.

nom: Phones at School: Should They Be Banned?
asl: Take the Test, Reading unit 3: Graffiti
stimul:
The following two letters were posted on a school internet forum under the topic “Phones at School.” (The letters were made up for learning purposes.)

Letter 1
Every break I see the same scene: dozens of students sitting in the hallway with their heads down, staring at their phones. Nobody talks to each other, and nobody kicks a ball in the schoolyard. When someone’s phone rings during a lesson, the whole class gets distracted. Last month two phones went missing in our class, and the parents blamed the teacher. And here is another bitter truth: some students secretly take photos of classmates, post them in group chats, and make fun of them. Why do we need all this trouble? School is a place for learning and making friends. Leave your phone at home or hand it in to the student on duty at the gate; the world will not change in one day! I ask the school administration to introduce a strict ban on phones.
Madina, Grade 9B

Letter 2
Banning is the easiest way. But is it the right way? My grandfather says that when he was at school, even bringing a calculator into class was forbidden: people said “children will forget how to calculate.” Today it is hard to imagine a physics or chemistry lesson without a calculator. A phone also contains a dictionary, maps, and electronic textbooks. Is the problem the device itself, or how we use it? Adults also stare at their phones in meetings, and nobody bans them. Instead of a ban, let’s write rules: during lessons, phones stay on silent and are used only when the teacher allows it; if a student breaks the rule, their phone stays with the homeroom teacher for the rest of the day. Times are changing; school should not fall behind.
Jasur, Grade 10A

nom: Is the Honey Genuine? The Lab Has the Answer
asl: Take the Test, Reading unit 6: Police
stimul:
(A popular science magazine article. The story in the introduction is fictional, but the method of analysis is real.)

[Introduction]
At a bazaar, a customer bought a jar of honey sold as “Bostanlyk mountain honey.” At home, she noticed that the honey was strangely runny and sweet like sugar syrup. The seller, however, insisted: “The honey is pure, I collected it in the mountains myself!” Who is right? How can this be proven?

Honey is the “signature” of flowers
When bees collect nectar from flowers, pollen, made up of very tiny grains, gets mixed into it. The grains are so small that they can only be seen under a microscope. The pollen of each plant species has its own particular shape: one looks like a spiky ball, another like a triangular grain. By looking at pollen, an expert can tell which plant it came from.

Same ingredients, different proportions
The pollen in honey can be compared to plov. Both Tashkent plov and Samarkand plov are made from rice, meat, carrots, and onions, but each uses these ingredients in different proportions, which is why an experienced cook can tell them apart by taste. Likewise, honey from two regions often contains pollen from the same plants, but the proportions are unique to each region. Mountain honey has a lot of pollen from wild grasses and shrubs, while honey from beside a cotton field is dominated by cotton pollen. In this way, the proportions of pollen act as a kind of “birth certificate” for honey.

[Box] How is pollen analysis carried out?
A lab technician dissolves about 10 grams of honey in warm water. The solution is spun quickly in a centrifuge, and the heavier pollen grains settle to the bottom of the test tube. The technician takes a drop of the sediment, spreads it on a glass slide, and, under a microscope, sorts and counts several hundred grains by type. The result is compared with reference honeys from different regions. If the “honey” contains almost no pollen, it has most likely been diluted with sugar syrup.

Only one piece of evidence
Pollen analysis is used more and more often in food quality control. But it does not always give the final verdict: for example, if honey is passed through a very fine filter, its pollen content also decreases. That is why experts also take into account the results of other tests, such as moisture and sugar content. Pollen analysis is just one of many pieces of evidence.

[Side box] What is pollen?
Pollen consists of tiny grains that flowering plants need in order to reproduce. Wind and insects carry them from one flower to another.

nom: A Load on Your Shoulders: Backpacks and Health
asl: Take the Test, Reading unit 7: Runners
stimul:
(An article from a school newspaper. The survey results are a made-up example.)

A LOAD ON YOUR SHOULDERS: IS YOUR BACKPACK A FRIEND TO YOUR HEALTH?
For our newspaper’s “Healthy Generation” column, Grade 9 students weighed the backpacks of 120 students at our school. This small survey is not a scientific study, but it gives us something to think about. The conclusion: what matters most is preventing the problem and having the right backpack.

Heavy bag, bent posture
Many pediatricians advise that a backpack should weigh no more than about 10 percent of a child’s body weight. Our survey showed that almost half of the students in Grades 5–6 carry a heavier load than this. A constant heavy load tires the muscles of the shoulders and lower back, and the child walks bent forward, which over time can lead to poor posture and back pain. Carrying a backpack on one shoulder is even more harmful: the body leans to one side.

Big or small?
If a backpack is too big, unnecessary things keep getting put into it: it gets heavier, hangs down below the waist, and pulls the body backward. If it is too small, the books do not fit, and the child carries the rest by hand. A good backpack should meet four requirements.
First, it should match the child’s height: its top edge should not rise above the shoulders, and its bottom edge should not hang below the waist.
Second, the shoulder straps should be wide and padded: thin straps dig into the shoulders and cause pain.
Third, the back panel should have a firm base and soft padding, so that the corners of books do not dig into the back.
Finally, the backpack should distribute the load evenly: it should have compartments inside, with heavy books placed close to the back; a waist belt is even better.

What should you do every day?
To avoid small but annoying problems such as back and shoulder pain and getting tired quickly, every evening you should check your timetable, pack only the books for the next day’s lessons, and wear your backpack on both shoulders.

nom: The Guest from the Snow (a story)
asl: Take the Test, Reading unit 8: The Gift
stimul:
THE GUEST FROM THE SNOW
(A story. The events and characters are fictional.)

For the third day, the snow would not stop. Grandma Oysha sat by the window watching the courtyard wall slowly disappear under a white wave. Few households still spent the winter in this remote village in the Nurata Mountains; her close neighbors had moved to their children’s homes in the city back in the autumn. Grandma should have left too. “One more week, until I finish selling the sheep,” she had told her son. And now there was no road, and the phone was silent.

At night the storm grew stronger. The snowdrift by the door rose to the windowsill in a single night. The roof creaked heavily, and the wind howled in the chimney. Grandma stirred the embers in the sandal, the low heated table, wrapped herself in the quilt, and fell asleep without noticing.

In the middle of the night a strange sound woke her: a long, painful sound, as if someone far away were moaning and weeping. Grandma jumped up. The sound came again, closer this time, weak and tired. Groping in the dark, she took down her late husband’s hunting rifle from the wall. “Who’s there?” she called. Instead of an answer, something moved through the snow on the porch, then began scratching at the door. Now Grandma knew: it was a wolf. A hungry wolf that had lost its pack in the storm.

When dawn broke, Grandma crept to the window. The wolf was lying at the edge of the porch, ice frozen in its fur, every rib showing. It did not look frightening; it looked pitiful. Just then the wolf suddenly leapt and threw itself at the window, and the glass shattered. Swallowing a scream, Grandma raised the rifle and fired. She missed. The wolf moved to the far corner of the porch and lay down again.

Toward noon, Grandma began to feel dizzy: she had eaten almost nothing for three days. She put the last of the dried meat in the pot and fried it. When the smell filled the house, a thin whining came from the porch. “Wait,” Grandma said to herself with a laugh, “first I’ll eat, and then I’ll take care of you too.” The wolf answered with a growl, and Grandma’s hand began to tremble.

After the meal, Grandma picked up the rifle again and went to the window. The wolf was still there: thin, exhausted, its eyes fixed on her. Grandma looked at it for a long time. Her fear had vanished somewhere. Then, without quite understanding what she was doing, she leaned the rifle against the wall, went into the kitchen, took the rest of the meat from the pot, and threw it out through the broken window. On the other side she heard a hungry growl. Grandma went back and sat on the bed, her heart pounding. “I’ve been hungry for three days too,” she whispered. Remembering the neighbors who had left, the shepherds stranded in the mountains, all this white silence, Grandma burst into tears for the first time since the snow had begun to fall.

The next morning, as soon as she opened her eyes, she sensed that something had changed. The snow had stopped, and the sky was bright blue. The sound of a tractor came from far away: they were clearing the road to the village. Grandma opened the door. The porch was empty. From the porch, tracks already fading in the sun led toward the juniper grove. And on the threshold lay a piece of bone, gnawed clean and white.

“THE POTTER’S SONG” (an excerpt from a play; the work was written for this task, and the events are fictional)

Summary: Master Hamid, an elderly potter from Rishtan, has not turned his potter’s wheel since his wife Oyshabibi died. Every evening Oyshabibi used to sing an old song called “Among the Gardens” next to the workshop, and the master would shape clay as she sang. The master’s daughter-in-law, Malika, has noticed that the voice of Dildora, a girl who sells pottery at the bazaar, is very much like the late Oyshabibi’s. Malika wants to bring her father-in-law back to life and back to his work.

(A courtyard. On the left, the door of the workshop; in the middle, a small supa — a raised wooden platform; on the right, two mulberry trees. The sun is setting.)

DILDORA. Sister, I still don’t understand. Who am I? I just sell pottery at the bazaar. How can a stranger’s voice ease a man’s grief?
MALIKA. Not the voice — the song. Only you can sing it.
DILDORA (puzzled). Me?
MALIKA. The first time I heard you at the bazaar, my heart skipped a beat. Aunt Oyshabibi sang the last verse exactly like that — low and unhurried. That song was when Father would begin shaping the clay.
(Silence. In the neighbor’s courtyard, the lid of a tandir oven clatters. Turtle doves coo.)
DILDORA (quietly). I’m sorry, sister, I can’t do it. It feels like a deception.
(She stands up and picks up her little basket.)
MALIKA (also in a tired voice). All right, my dear. Forgive me.
(From inside the workshop comes the creak of the potter’s wheel. Malika gives a start.)
MALIKA. Did you hear that? He has touched the wheel for the first time in a year! Please, just once... Sit on the supa and sing “Among the Gardens.” Tomorrow I will explain everything myself, even if he is upset.
DILDORA (in a whisper). Which verse should I start with?
MALIKA (squeezing her hand tightly). The last one.
(Malika slips into the darkness between the mulberry trees and hides. Dildora sits on the supa and sings softly. The workshop door opens. Master Hamid, his hands covered in clay, stops in the doorway.)
MASTER HAMID. Who... who is singing?
DILDORA (stopping the song). Forgive me, grandpa. I was on my way home from the bazaar.
MASTER HAMID (after a long silence, gently). You sang well, my child. If you pass by at this time tomorrow too... I will oil the wheel.
(He goes back inside, leaving the door open. The sound of the wheel begins, steady and even. Malika comes out of the darkness.)
DILDORA (after a while, quietly). He didn’t recognize me...
MALIKA. It was dark... And besides, who knows what voice he hears in his dreams now? (Shyly.) The last bus has gone, my dear. Will you stay with us tonight?
DILDORA (in a strange voice). All right, sister.
(It becomes completely dark. Only the steady creaking of the wheel can be heard.)
CURTAIN

Some jobs in the theater
Actor — creates a character on stage: speaks and sings as the character.
Director — is in charge of all parts of the production: decides where the actors stand on stage and when they enter and exit, and decides how the play is to be interpreted.

Sound operator — is responsible for all the sound effects in the play (birdsong, a creaking door, wind); stays at the control desk throughout the performance.

asl: Take the Test, Reading unit 11: New Rules
stimul:
EDITORIAL
(The text was written for learning purposes; the events and names in it are fictional.)

The digital world needs new rules

Technology often stays one step ahead of law and ethics. When cars first appeared on the streets at the beginning of the 20th century, there were no traffic rules yet; the rules were written in a hurry only after collisions became more common. Today a similar situation is repeating itself in our digital lives.

Most of us think of the photos on our phones, our messages and the documents in our cloud storage as our own. But who do they go to when their owner dies?

Recently one family was faced with exactly this question. A young artist, Kamola, and her husband, Sardor, were killed in a car accident. Hundreds of Kamola’s paintings — ten years of her work — were stored only in her account on a cloud service. Kamola’s parents wanted to put the paintings on display in an exhibition, while Sardor’s brother suggested selling them. The service provider would not open the account to anyone: the user had not given permission for this while she was alive.

Who gets the paintings? If the account is opened, won’t her private messages be opened too? Or should the account simply be deleted? Naturally, Kamola and Sardor had never thought about such a situation in advance.

To study the issue, a special commission was set up, made up of lawyers, information technology specialists and representatives of the artists’ union. Last week the commission announced its conclusion: the paintings should go to the legal heirs as an inheritance, but the private messages should not be opened, because the owner had not consented to this.

Realizing how sensitive the issue is, the members of the commission did not put the conclusion into effect immediately: the public was given two months to express its views. If there are many objections, the conclusion will be reconsidered.

Now every user opening an account with this company is asked to decide in advance what should be done with their data after their death.

This ensures that what happened to Kamola and Sardor will not happen again. But what about other questions? In another family, the voice and appearance of a deceased blogger were “brought back to life” using artificial intelligence, and advertising videos began to be made in his name; the family had to go to court to stop this. Who owns a deceased person’s voice and appearance? Who may distribute such an AI-generated video, when, and on what terms?

In the age of the automobile, many accidents happened because the rules came too late. The opportunities for misusing digital technologies are even greater. Ethical and legal boundaries must be set before we go too far.

stimul:
THE JUST JUDGE
(Written in the spirit of Uzbek folk tales; the story is fictional.)

Long, long ago, so the story goes, there lived a ruler named Sultan Mahmudkhan. People told him: “In a city far from the capital there is a judge who finds the truth at once — no cheat can hide from him.” The khan wanted to see this with his own eyes. He put on the clothes of an ordinary merchant, mounted his horse and set off alone for that city.

By the pool next to the city gate, the khan got off his horse to wash his face. Just then a traveler came up and said: “Brother, let me hold your horse while you wash in peace.” The khan handed him the reins. When he straightened up, they say, the traveler was already sitting on the horse.
“Get down and give me back my horse!” said the khan.
“What horse? This is my horse! If you don’t believe me, come to the judge!” shouted the traveler.
The people who had gathered around also said: “Go to the judge, he will settle it!”

There was a long line at the courthouse. Two women went in before the khan. Each of them claimed that the same carpet was “mine.” The judge listened to them both, was silent for a while, and then said: “Leave the carpet here and come back tomorrow.”
Then a halva seller and a coal seller came in. The halva seller was clutching a purse, and the coal seller was holding him by the sleeve.
“This purse is mine, and the coal man tried to snatch it,” said the halva seller.
“That’s a lie!” said the coal seller. “I was counting the coins I had earned selling coal all day, and he grabbed my purse and ran.”
The judge said: “Leave the purse here and come back tomorrow.”
Then it was the khan’s turn. He told what had happened. But the traveler said: “This man begged me on the road and offered to hold my horse, and now he says my horse is his.” The judge had the horse left there too, and ordered them to come back the next day.

The next day the whole city gathered at the courthouse. The judge gave the carpet to a woman named Zebiniso and sentenced the other woman to forty days of cleaning the city’s irrigation ditches. Then he returned the purse to the coal seller and also sentenced the halva seller to forty days of cleaning ditches.
Finally, the judge took the khan and the traveler to the door of a stable where twenty horses stood and said: “Each of you, call your horse once.” When the traveler called, the horse did not stir. But when the khan whistled, the horse neighed and came straight to him. The judge handed the horse over to the khan and sentenced the traveler, too, to forty days of cleaning ditches.

In the evening the khan went to the judge’s house.
“Are you unhappy with my verdict?” asked the judge.
“I am satisfied,” said the khan. “Only explain to me how you knew.”
“Here is how I found out about the carpet: during the night I asked each woman separately, ‘What is woven in which corner of the carpet?’ Zebiniso answered at once: ‘In the bottom left corner there is a small pomegranate — I weave it into every carpet I make as my mark.’ The other woman did not know. I spread out the carpet and looked — the pomegranate was right there.
Here is how I found out about the purse: I put the coins in a bowl of water. In the morning the water had turned dark, and coal dust had settled at the bottom. If the coins had belonged to the halva seller, the water would not have turned dark.
The matter of the horse was harder. Both of you knew the horse. But I wanted to find out not which of you knew the horse, but which of you the horse knew.”
Then the khan said: “I am not a merchant — I am Sultan Mahmudkhan. What they say about you is true. Ask for whatever you wish.”
“I need no reward,” said the judge. “My ruler’s praise is enough for me.”

CYBERBULLYING: PARENTS AND TEACHERS OFTEN UNAWARE
(The article was written for learning purposes; the survey and the figures are hypothetical.)

According to the results of a survey released on Wednesday by the regional Department of Public Education, only one in three children who have experienced harassment and humiliation online (cyberbullying) has parents who know about it.

The survey was conducted in November–December 2025 in schools where cases of cyberbullying had been reported. Nearly 12 thousand parents, teachers and students in grades 4–11 took part. This was the first time the department had carried out such a survey.

Fifteen percent of students in grades 4–6 described themselves as victims of cyberbullying; the figure was 24 percent in grades 7–9 and 17 percent in grades 10–11. At the same time, 8 percent of students in grades 4–6, 19 percent in grades 7–9 and 12 percent in grades 10–11 admitted that they had humiliated others online. Of those who had humiliated others, 40–55 percent said that they themselves had been humiliated before.

Among students in grades 4–6 who had been cyberbullied, 41 percent of their parents knew about it. In grades 7–9 the figure was 30 percent, and in grades 10–11, 19 percent. Of the parents who knew, 20–25 percent had heard about it from a teacher, and only 5–7 percent from their own child.

The survey showed that most teachers are also unaware: 38 percent of teachers who teach grades 4–6 are unaware of cyberbullying aimed at their students. This share is 24 percent among teachers of grades 7–9 and 61 percent among teachers of grades 10–11.

When asked about the causes of cyberbullying, nearly 70 percent of teachers pointed to the lack of control over children’s phone use at home. Most parents, however, saw a lack of empathy and a sense of fairness in children as the main cause.

According to a department representative, the results show that parents and teachers need to communicate with children more often and more openly.

The issue of cyberbullying began to be widely discussed in the region last fall: a 7th-grade student stayed away from school for two months after classmates spread a humiliating video on social media, and the family was forced to move to another district. After this incident, the department sent schools guidelines on preventing cyberbullying and decided to carry out this survey.

The following information is taken from a booklet about silk production (the text was written for learning purposes).

HOW A COCOON IS SPUN
The silkworm feeds only on mulberry leaves. The tiny caterpillar that hatches from the egg eats leaves nonstop for about a month, and during this time it sheds its skin four times. Each time before shedding its skin, the caterpillar goes without food for about a day and stays still with its head raised — silkworm breeders say that “the worm has gone to sleep.”

You can tell that a caterpillar is ready to spin its cocoon by two signs: it stops eating leaves completely, and its body turns yellowish and almost transparent. Then the breeders put dry twigs next to the caterpillars. The caterpillar climbs onto a twig and, constantly swinging its head in a figure-eight pattern, produces a fine thread from its mouth and wraps itself in it. This takes 2–3 days. The thread of one cocoon is one unbroken piece and can be a thousand meters long or even longer.

GETTING SILK FROM COCOONS
After about two weeks, the pupa inside the cocoon turns into a moth and breaks out through the cocoon. When this happens, the thread is broken in many places and can no longer be unwound in one piece. That is why the finished cocoons are dried with hot air or steam.

The cocoon thread is stuck together by a glue-like substance called sericin. At a silk-reeling factory the cocoons are put into hot water: the sericin softens, making it easier to find the end of the thread and unwind it. Because the thread of a single cocoon is very thin, the threads of 5–8 cocoons are unwound together and made into one thread of raw silk. Later the raw silk is boiled to remove the sericin, and it becomes soft and shiny.

Silk is used to weave atlas and adras fabrics, silk headscarves and carpets.

GLOSSARY
pupa — the stage of the caterpillar inside the cocoon before it turns into a moth.
silk reeler — a craftsman who unwinds thread from cocoons.

nom: Ozone in the Sky over Tashkent
asl: Take the Test, Science unit 2: Ozone
stimul:
On hot, windless summer days in Tashkent, you may sometimes hear about an “ozone alert.” What is ozone, and why is it sometimes called useful and sometimes harmful?

An ordinary oxygen molecule (O₂) is made of two oxygen atoms, while an ozone molecule (O₃) is made of three oxygen atoms. There is very little ozone in the air: fewer than ten out of every million molecules are ozone.

Where ozone is located matters. The layer from the Earth’s surface up to a height of about 10–12 km is the troposphere. Ozone here is called “bad ozone”: it forms from gases in road and factory emissions under the action of sunlight, irritates the airways, makes asthma attacks worse and damages plant leaves.

Above the troposphere, up to a height of about 50 km, is the stratosphere. About 90 percent of the ozone in the atmosphere is found here. This “good ozone” absorbs most of the dangerous ultraviolet rays (UV-B) coming from the Sun. If this layer becomes thinner, more UV-B reaches the Earth’s surface, and certain diseases become more common in people.

In the stratosphere, ozone is both formed and broken down every day. How it forms is shown in the picture.

nom: Daytime in Tashkent and Cape Town
asl: Take the Test, Science unit 3: Daylight
stimul:
On June 21, the Northern Hemisphere has the longest day of the year. In Tashkent (about 41° north latitude), the sun rises at about 4:49 and sets at 19:59 on that day: daytime lasts 15 hours 10 minutes.

On the same day, in Cape Town, South Africa (about 34° south latitude), it is the shortest day of the year: the sun rises at 7:51 and sets at 17:44, so daytime lasts only 9 hours 53 minutes.

On December 21, it is the other way around: daytime in Tashkent lasts about 9 hours 11 minutes, and in Cape Town 14 hours 25 minutes.

Astronomers explain that the seasons are reversed in the two hemispheres because the Earth’s axis is tilted about 23.5° from the line perpendicular to the plane of the Earth’s orbit. (Times are local times, calculated and rounded.)

nom: A Copy of a Karakul Lamb
asl: Take the Test, Science unit 4: Cloning
stimul:
Imagine that the following simplified article appeared in a science magazine (the method is real, the situation is made up).

“A black Karakul ram cloned in the laboratory”

Scientists took a very small skin sample from the ear of a rare black Karakul ram (Sheep 1). From the sample they separated one “tiny piece” and drew out its nucleus with a micro-needle.

Then they took an egg cell from another, white ewe (Sheep 2) and first removed its own nucleus — that is, the material that determines the characteristics of the future lamb. The nucleus taken from Sheep 1 was placed into the empty egg cell.

After this cell had divided for several days and become a small embryo, it was placed in the uterus of a third ewe (Sheep 3). Sheep 3 became pregnant and, five months later, gave birth to a black lamb. The scientists named it “Copy.”

The article ends like this: “Some scientists believe that in the future it may also be possible to clone humans. However, many countries have banned human cloning by law.”

asl: Take the Test, Science unit 5: Greenhouse
stimul:
A made-up situation (the data have been simplified for learning purposes).

The PM2.5 indicator is often used to assess air pollution: these are tiny particles with a diameter of less than 2.5 micrometers. They penetrate deep into the lungs. The particles enter the air from car exhaust, burning coal and wood, construction dust and dust storms. How many particles stay in the air also depends on the weather: wind and rain clean the air, while on cold, windless days the particles build up over the city.

Jasur, a grade 9 student, found two graphs about a regional center: the number of registered cars by year and the annual average amount of PM2.5 in the air.

Looking at the graphs, Jasur concluded: “It is clear that the increase in PM2.5 is caused by the growing number of cars.”

asl: Take the Test, Science unit 6: Clothes
stimul:
A made-up news story.

A team of young engineers, residents of the IT Park in Tashkent, is developing a “smart” heated vest for builders and road workers who work outdoors in winter.

The vest is made of ordinary cotton fabric with a mesh of thin carbon fibers woven into it. These fibers conduct electric current. When current from a small battery in the pocket flows through the fibers, they heat up and warm the fabric to 40 °C. A temperature sensor inside the fabric switches off the current if the vest gets too hot.

Team leader Shohruh says: “The main innovation is the way we weave the fibers into the fabric. From the outside, the vest looks no different from ordinary clothing.”

According to the developers’ claims, once the battery is removed, the vest can be washed in a washing machine, ironed, and rolled up and put in a bag — the fabric is not damaged. They also point out that the vest can be mass-produced at a low price.

asl: Take the Test, Science unit 7: The Grand Canyon
stimul:
Imagine that geologists are studying a deep canyon cut by a river in a mountainous area in the south of Uzbekistan. In some places the canyon is up to 400 meters deep. Long ago, movements of the Earth’s crust lifted the rock layers upward, and then, over millions of years, the river carved through them and formed the canyon.

Different rock layers can be clearly seen in the canyon walls (see the diagram). In this area, daytime temperatures in summer rise above +40 °C, and nighttime temperatures in winter drop to −15 °C. Despite the dry climate, rain and snowmelt water sometimes get into cracks in the rocks.

Thousands of tourists visit the canyon every year. Local residents are worried that so many people walking there is harming nature.

asl: Take the Test, Science unit 9: Mary Montagu
stimul:
From the history of vaccines

Rabies is a disease caused by a virus, usually transmitted when a rabid animal bites. Once symptoms appear, it almost always ends in death.

In the 1880s, the French scientist Louis Pasteur worked on weakening the agent that causes rabies. He dried the spinal cords of infected rabbits for several days, which weakened the agent, and tested this material by injecting it into dogs. In July 1885, a mother brought her 9-year-old son, Joseph Meister, who had been badly bitten by a rabid dog, to Pasteur. Over several days, Pasteur and the doctors injected the boy with stronger and stronger material. Joseph did not get sick and stayed healthy.

Today, in many countries, including Uzbekistan, children are vaccinated against measles, polio, hepatitis B and other diseases according to the national immunization schedule.

asl: Take the Test, Science unit 10: Acid Rain
stimul:
Many historic buildings, statues and gravestones are made of marble or limestone. The main component of these rocks is calcium carbonate (CaCO₃). In industrial cities, the surfaces of such monuments are seen to become rough over a few decades, and their inscriptions fade. Scientists point to acid rain as the cause.

Ordinary rainwater is also slightly acidic, because it dissolves carbon dioxide (CO₂) from the air. Acid rain, however, is even more acidic, because sulfur oxides and nitrogen oxides are also dissolved in it.

Members of a chemistry club made a model of the effect of acid rain on limestone. They placed small pieces of limestone in food vinegar overnight (vinegar is slightly more acidic than acid rain, so the process goes faster). As soon as the limestone was put into the vinegar, gas bubbles appeared on its surface. The mass of the dried piece was measured before and after the experiment.

asl: Take the Test, Science unit 11: Physical Exercise
stimul:
Every year an international marathon is held in Tashkent, and thousands of amateurs also run the 5 km or 10 km distances. Sixteen-year-old Aziz decided to train for three months for the race: running at a moderate pace for 30–40 minutes three times a week.

Doctors point out that regular but moderate physical exercise is good for health.

asl: Take the Test, Science unit 12: Genetically Modified Crops
stimul:
An imaginary situation.

“GM cotton should be banned”

Nature conservation organizations are demanding a ban on a new genetically modified (GM) variety of cotton. This GM cotton was created to be resistant to a powerful new herbicide that kills ordinary cotton. The new herbicide kills almost all the weeds in cotton fields.

Naturalists say that weeds are a food source for insects and for the birds that feed on them, so using GM cotton together with the new herbicide will harm nature. Supporters of GM cotton say that a scientific study has shown this will not happen.

Details of the study:
• The cotton was planted in 150 fields in different regions of the country (Fergana, Kashkadarya, Syrdarya, Khorezm and others).
• Each field was divided into two equal parts. In one part, GM cotton sprayed with the new herbicide was grown; in the other part, ordinary cotton sprayed with the usual herbicide was grown.
• The number of insects in the GM cotton areas sprayed with the new herbicide turned out to be almost the same as the number of insects in the ordinary cotton areas sprayed with the usual herbicide.

asl: Take the Test, Science unit 13: Biodiversity
stimul:
“Biodiversity — the key to protecting nature”

The tugai forests along the Amu Darya and Syr Darya rivers are a unique ecosystem made up of Euphrates poplar, tamarisk and reed beds. Many different insects, birds, reptiles and mammals live here. In recent decades, the area of tugai forests has shrunk considerably because of decreasing river water and land development.

Ecologists believe that an ecosystem with high biodiversity (that is, many species of living organisms) can adapt better to changes caused by human activity than an ecosystem with low diversity.

The picture shows two simplified food webs. Each arrow points from the organism that is eaten to the organism that eats it. Food web A is a tugai forest with high diversity: it has many alternative ways of getting food. Food web B is a damaged area with low diversity: at some levels, the food chain passes through only one species.

The loss of biodiversity is a serious problem: not only are the lost species a great loss in themselves, but the remaining species also become more likely to disappear in the future.

The food webs as text (who ← eats what):
A: Aphid ← Poplar, Tamarisk; Caterpillar ← Poplar; Grasshopper ← Reed, Tamarisk; Spider ← Grasshopper, Aphid; Ladybug ← Aphid, Caterpillar; Lizard ← Spider, Grasshopper; Sparrow ← Caterpillar, Grasshopper, Ladybug; Snake ← Lizard, Sparrow; Fox ← Lizard, Sparrow, Grasshopper.
B: Aphid ← Tamarisk; Grasshopper ← Tamarisk; Ladybug ← Aphid; Sparrow ← Ladybug; Lizard ← Grasshopper; Fox ← Sparrow; Snake ← Sparrow, Lizard.

asl: Take the Test, Science unit 16: Flies
stimul:
A made-up situation.

Rustam, a farmer in the Tashkent region, grows tomatoes in a large greenhouse. One year, whiteflies — tiny insects that suck plant sap — multiplied so much in the greenhouse that the tomato leaves turned yellow and the harvest began to shrink. Rustam sprayed the plants with a solution of insecticide A. The insecticide killed almost all the whiteflies.

However, a month later the whiteflies multiplied again. Rustam sprayed again, and the result was similar to the first time: most of the whiteflies died, but not all of them. This happened five times, and each time insecticide A became less and less effective.

Rustam remembered that at the beginning of the season he had prepared the solution for all the sprayings in one large container. So he suggested: “Perhaps the solution has gone bad over time and become weaker.”

asl: Take the Test, Science unit 17: Calf Clones
stimul:
An imaginary science news story (the method is real, the situation is made up).

Scientists at a livestock research laboratory succeeded in producing four kids (baby goats) with the same genetic material — clones. Although the kids were born to four different goats, their genetic material is identical.

First, the scientists took about twenty egg cells from a goat named Oqbosh-1 and removed the nucleus from each egg cell.

Then they took an early embryo of about twenty cells from another goat (Oqbosh-2). They separated the embryo into individual cells and took the nucleus out of each cell. Each nucleus was injected separately into one of the egg cells without a nucleus taken from Oqbosh-1.

Finally, the twenty egg cells with injected nuclei were placed in twenty surrogate (substitute) goats. Five months later, four of them each gave birth to one kid.

One of the researchers said that using this method widely could be economically profitable for livestock breeding.

asl: Take the Test, Science unit 18: Corn
stimul:
Bakhtiyor, a farmer from Jizzakh, collects the straw left in the field after the wheat harvest, presses it and turns it into small pellets. In winter he burns these pellets in his stove to heat his house. "Pellets burn evenly and with little smoke," he says.

Straw has long been given to livestock as feed. According to Bakhtiyor, feed is actually a kind of fuel too: a cow eats straw and gets energy from it. The farmer thinks that in the future, selling straw as fuel rather than as feed could bring in more income.

The district ecologist, however, objects: whenever any plant material burns, carbon dioxide (CO₂) is released, and CO₂ is one of the gases that strengthen the greenhouse effect. Bakhtiyor replies: "While plants grow, they absorb CO₂ from the air and release oxygen. The field will take back the CO₂ from the straw I burn next year."

(The conversation is made up, but making fuel pellets from straw and other plant residues is a real practice.)

asl: Take the Test, Science unit 19: Fit for Drinking
stimul:
In many cities, including Tashkent, part of the drinking water is taken from rivers and canals. Before this water reaches homes, it is cleaned in several stages at a water treatment plant (simplified diagram):

1) Screen — large debris such as branches and plastic bottles is caught.
2) Settling tank — water flows very slowly through a large basin for several hours.
3) Sand filter — water seeps through a thick layer of sand.
4) Disinfection — a small amount of chlorine is added to the water.
5) Laboratory — water quality is checked, and then the water is sent to homes through pipes.

asl: Take the Test, Science unit 20: Tooth Decay
stimul:
To make yogurt, a little ready-made yogurt (a starter) is added to warm milk. The starter contains lactic acid bacteria. Today this process is well understood:

• The bacteria feed on the milk sugar in milk, called lactose.
• Lactose is turned into lactic acid.
• The acid makes the milk protein, casein, curdle, so the milk thickens and the yogurt gets a sour taste.

Diagram: lactose (1) —bacteria→ lactic acid (2) → casein curdles, thick yogurt (3)

nom: A Car in the Summer Heat
asl: Take the Test, Science unit 21: Hot Work
stimul: Jasur, a repairman from Termez, is busy with repair jobs in the summer. He left a plastic bottle of water, a set of metal wrenches and a wooden ruler in the trunk of his car. After the car stood in the sun for several hours, the air temperature inside the trunk reached about 55 °C.

asl: Take the Test, Science unit 22: Mousepox
stimul:
Locusts (for example, the Moroccan locust and the migratory locust) cause great damage to crops and pastures in many regions of Uzbekistan. In nature there are species of fungi that infect mainly locusts and their relatives only; biological products are made from them.

Suppose (the situation is made up) that a laboratory changed the DNA of such a fungus by genetic engineering and created a new strain that kills locusts much faster. The scientists say this is necessary to protect crops. Critics, however, worry that the modified fungus could spread from the laboratory and infect other insects as well — for example, honeybees, which pollinate many crops.

asl: Take the Test, Science unit 23: Stickleback Behaviour
stimul:
The betta (Siamese fighting fish) is an easy fish to keep in an aquarium. The male has long, wide fins, while the female's fins are shorter. During the breeding season, the female's belly fills with eggs and becomes round.

A male betta attacks any other male that enters its territory: it spreads its gill covers and rushes at it. If a female full of eggs approaches, the male "dances" around her and invites her to his bubble nest on the surface of the water.

A student wants to find out what causes the male fish's aggression. There is one male fish in the aquarium. The student made three wax models of the same color and size but with fins of different lengths. He hung the models on a wire, lowered them into the aquarium one at a time for the same length of time, and counted how many times the male fish attacked each model. The results are shown in the graph (results of the student's experiment).

asl: Take the Test, Science unit 24: Tobacco Smoking
stimul:
Naswar (nasvay) is a mixture made from ground tobacco, slaked lime, ash and other additives. People put it under the tongue or behind the lip. The nicotine in naswar is absorbed into the blood through the lining of the mouth, quickly reaches the brain and causes addiction (dependence). The lime constantly irritates the lining of the mouth.

Research has shown that people who use naswar have a higher risk of diseases of the mouth, including mouth cancer. In Uzbekistan, selling naswar and other tobacco products to minors is prohibited by law.

asl: Take the Test, Science unit 25: Starlight
stimul: Every year in mid-August, the Earth passes through the Perseid meteor shower: in a dark sky you can see up to several dozen "shooting stars" per hour. One night, Malika from Tashkent saw only a few meteors from the roof of her house in the city center. The next night she went with her family to a village at the foot of the Chimgan mountains, and there she saw many more meteors, including faint ones.

asl: Take the Test, Science unit 26: Ultrasound
stimul:
Sardor, a 15-year-old student at a sports school, is having a medical checkup. The doctor examines his heart using ultrasound (echocardiography). A probe is placed on his chest and sends very high-frequency sound waves, which the human ear cannot hear, into the body. The waves bounce back (echo) from the walls and valves of the heart. The probe receives the returning waves, and a computer builds an image from them.

Ultrasound travels through the soft tissues of the body at a speed of about 1540 m/s. This kind of examination is considered safe and is widely used for children and pregnant women.

asl: Take the Test, Science unit 27: Lip Gloss
stimul:
Below are recipes for two kinds of homemade lip balm. Stick balm is hard, while balm in a jar is soft and easy to apply.

Soft balm in a jar:
• 8 g cottonseed oil
• 2 g beeswax
• 1 g cocoa butter
• 2 drops peppermint essential oil

Stick balm:
• 8 g cottonseed oil
• 5 g beeswax
• 1 g cocoa butter
• 2 drops peppermint essential oil

Method (the same for both): put the oil, wax and cocoa butter in a small container and melt them over hot water (in a water bath) until the mixture is smooth. Then add the essential oil, stir and pour into a mold.

asl: Take the Test, Science unit 28: Evolution
stimul:
Modern whales live only in water, and their hind legs cannot be seen from the outside. Scientists have found fossil skeletons of animals that resemble whales and are thought to be their ancestors, and they have determined when these animals lived. The table gives information about three of them and about the modern whale (ages are rounded).

Pakicetus — about 50 million years ago — lived mainly on land, near water — had four fully developed legs that easily carried its body.
Ambulocetus — about 49 million years ago — lived in shallow water and on the shore — four shorter legs, with large feet adapted for swimming.
Basilosaurus — about 40–34 million years ago — lived only in the sea — its front legs had become flippers, and its hind legs were very small compared with its body and were useless for walking.
Modern whale — present day — only in water — front legs are flippers, there are no hind legs on the outside, and inside the body there is only a small remnant of a pelvic bone.

asl: Take the Test, Science unit 29: Bread Dough
stimul: In a science club, students put warm water, a spoonful of sugar and dry yeast into a glass bottle and stretched a deflated rubber balloon over the mouth of the bottle. Yeast is a single-celled fungus. It breaks down sugar and turns it into carbon dioxide (CO₂) and ethyl alcohol; this process is called fermentation. After 30–40 minutes, the balloon slowly began to inflate.

asl: Take the Test, Science unit 30: Transit of Venus
stimul:
On October 25, 2022, a partial solar eclipse was seen in Uzbekistan: the Moon passed between the Earth and the Sun and covered part of the Sun's disk. Students in Samarkand observed the eclipse with the school telescope: they pointed the telescope at the Sun and projected the image coming out of the eyepiece onto a white piece of cardboard (the projection method). On the cardboard, the dark part of the Sun's disk covered by the Moon could be seen clearly.

Sometimes planets also pass between an observer and the Sun and move across the Sun's disk as a small dark spot. This event is called a transit. For example, a transit of Venus was seen from the Earth in 2012.

asl: Take the Test, Science unit 31: Health Risk?
stimul:
Imagine that you live in a small town near a large cement factory (the situation is made up). In recent years, more people in the town have gone to the doctor with chronic coughs and asthma. Many residents think the cause is the dust and gases coming out of the factory chimneys.

At a meeting about this issue, scientists made the following statements.

Scientists working for the factory: "We tested water samples taken from wells in the town. No toxic substances were found in them."

Scientists working for the residents: "We compared the number of people registered with chronic respiratory diseases in the town with the number of such patients in another district 100 km from the factory. There are more such patients near the factory."

asl: Take the Test, Science unit 32: Catalytic Converter
stimul:
The smoke from coal-fired thermal power plants contains sulfur dioxide (SO₂). It inflames the airways and forms acid rain in the atmosphere. That is why, in modern power plants, the smoke is passed through a cleaning unit before it goes up the chimney: the smoke passes through a mixture of crushed limestone (CaCO₃) and water. About 90 percent of the SO₂, with the help of oxygen, turns into a solid substance — gypsum — and is trapped. A small amount of extra CO₂ is also produced in the process.

Gases entering the unit with the smoke: nitrogen N₂; oxygen O₂; carbon dioxide CO₂; water vapor H₂O; sulfur dioxide SO₂ (100%).
Gases going out of the chimney: nitrogen N₂; oxygen O₂ (slightly less); carbon dioxide CO₂ (slightly more); water vapor H₂O; sulfur dioxide SO₂ (10%).
Trapped in the unit: gypsum CaSO₄·2H₂O (90% of the sulfur in the SO₂ ends up here).

asl: Take the Test, Science unit 33: Major Surgery
stimul: Appendicitis is an inflammation of the appendix (the worm-shaped extension of the cecum); it is often treated with surgery. Major operations are carried out in specially equipped operating rooms. Before the operation, the patient is given general anesthesia, and after the operation, the patient stays in the hospital under observation for several days.

asl: Take the Test, Science unit 34: Wind Farms
stimul: Many people think that electricity should be produced using wind instead of coal and gas. Large wind power plants are being built in Uzbekistan too, especially in the Navoi region and Karakalpakstan. The wind turns the blades of a turbine, the blades drive a generator, and electricity is produced.
